questions.q: A bronchus is identified in a lung section. Which histological feature distinguishes an intrapulmonary bronchus from a bronchiole?
options: A simple squamous epithelial lining throughout
questions.explain: Intrapulmonary bronchi contain irregular cartilage plates and submucosal glands; bronchioles lack cartilage and submucosal glands.

questions.q: A small airway has no cartilage or submucosal glands and is lined mainly by ciliated cuboidal cells with club cells. What is it?
questions.explain: Bronchioles are small conducting airways without cartilage or submucosal glands; their epithelium becomes lower and includes club cells.

questions.q: Which cell type produces pulmonary surfactant and can proliferate to replace damaged alveolar epithelial cells?
questions.explain: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant and serve as progenitor cells capable of differentiating into type I and type II alveolar cells.

questions.q: Which alveolar cell forms most of the extremely thin surface across which oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse?
questions.explain: Type I pneumocytes are thin squamous cells covering most of the alveolar surface and forming the epithelial component of the blood–air barrier.

questions.q: A lung section shows a dust-laden phagocytic cell within an alveolar space. Which cell is this?
questions.explain: Alveolar macrophages migrate over the alveolar surface and phagocytose inhaled particles and microorganisms; they are also called dust cells.

questions.q: Which sequence best represents the principal layers crossed by oxygen moving from alveolar air into pulmonary capillary blood?
options: Type I pneumocyte, fused epithelial and endothelial basal laminae, capillary endothelium
Type II pneumocyte, cartilage, capillary smooth muscle
Ciliated columnar epithelium, submucosal gland, venous endothelium
Alveolar macrophage, elastic cartilage, capillary endothelium
questions.explain: The thin blood–air barrier consists principally of type I alveolar epithelium, closely apposed/fused basal laminae and capillary endothelium, providing a short diffusion distance.

questions.q: A terminal bronchiole is identified in a lung section. Which epithelial cell is particularly important for secretion of protective proteins and detoxification of inhaled substances in this airway?
questions.explain: Club (formerly Clara) cells are non-ciliated secretory cells in bronchioles. They contribute protective secretions, metabolise inhaled compounds and act as progenitor cells for bronchiolar epithelium.

questions.q: A section of trachea shows respiratory epithelium overlying a broad band of hyaline cartilage. What is the typical shape of the tracheal cartilage rings?
options: C-shaped rings with posterior gaps bridged by trachealis muscle
Small isolated cartilage nodules arranged in a spiral
questions.explain: Tracheal hyaline cartilage forms C-shaped rings that are open posteriorly, where the trachealis smooth muscle and connective tissue lie adjacent to the oesophagus.

questions.q: Which histological change is expected as the airway branches from a bronchus into smaller bronchioles?
options: Cartilage plates and submucosal glands disappear
The epithelium becomes stratified squamous throughout
The smooth muscle layer disappears completely
Alveoli are present in the wall of every terminal bronchiole
questions.explain: Bronchioles lack cartilage and submucosal glands. Their epithelium becomes progressively lower, while smooth muscle remains prominent; alveoli begin to appear in respiratory bronchioles.

questions.q: A histological section shows an alveolar septum containing numerous small vascular channels and elastic fibres. Which vessel type forms the dense capillary network closely applied to the alveolar epithelium?
questions.explain: Pulmonary capillaries form an extensive network within alveolar septa and lie close to type I pneumocytes, facilitating gas exchange. Elastic fibres support recoil of the lung.
